title: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple
description: Distinguish between finished past actions and actions connected to the present.

rules.title: Past Simple: Definite Finished Time
rules.explanation: Use Past Simple when an action happened at a specific, finished time in the past (yesterday, last year, in 2020, 2 days ago).
rules.exampleIncorrect: I have visited London last summer.

rules.title: Present Perfect: Life Experience & Unfinished Time
rules.explanation: Use Present Perfect when the time is not mentioned, or the period is still ongoing (today, this week, ever, never, already, yet).
rules.exampleCorrect: I have visited London three times in my life.
rules.exampleIncorrect: I visited London three times in my life (when talking about life experience).

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct verb form: "She ___ her keys yesterday evening."
exercises.explanation: "Yesterday evening" specifies a finished time, demanding Past Simple ("lost").

options: Have you ever seen a shooting star?
Did you ever saw a shooting star in your life?
Have you ever saw a shooting star?
Are you ever seeing a shooting star?
exercises.explanation: "Have you ever + past participle" asks about lifetime experiences.

title: Conditionals (Zero, First & Second)
description: Form logical if-statements ranging from scientific facts to real and imaginary possibilities.
formula: If + Present, Future (1st) | If + Past, Would + Verb (2nd)

rules.title: Zero Conditional (General Truths)
rules.explanation: If + present simple, present simple. Used for universal scientific facts and invariable routines.
rules.exampleCorrect: If you heat ice, it melts.
rules.exampleIncorrect: If you will heat ice, it will melt.

rules.title: First Conditional (Real Future Possibility)
rules.explanation: If + present simple, will + base verb. Used for likely future consequences.
rules.exampleCorrect: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
rules.exampleIncorrect: If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay home.

rules.title: Second Conditional (Hypothetical / Imaginary)
rules.explanation: If + past simple, would + base verb. Used for unreal present/future dreams.
rules.exampleCorrect: If I won a million dollars, I would travel the world.
rules.exampleIncorrect: If I will win a million dollars, I will travel.

exercises.prompt: "If I ___ you, I would take that prestigious job offer."
exercises.explanation: In hypothetical Second Conditional advice, "If I were you" is the standard subjunctive form.

exercises.prompt: "If she studies diligently, she ___ all her exams next month."
exercises.explanation: First conditional structure: If + present, will + infinitive.

title: Modal Verbs of Deduction
description: Express varying degrees of certainty about present and past events.
formula: Must / Can't / Might / Could + Base Verb (Present) or + Have + V3 (Past)

rules.title: Certainty (Must vs. Can't)
rules.explanation: Use 'must' when 99% sure something is true. Use 'can't' (or 'couldn't') when 99% sure it is impossible. Never say 'must not' for impossibility.
rules.exampleCorrect: His lights are off; he must be sleeping.
rules.exampleIncorrect: His lights are on; he must not be home.

rules.title: Possibility (Might / May / Could)
rules.explanation: Use 'might', 'may', or 'could' when something is possible but not certain (around 50% chance).
rules.exampleCorrect: Take an umbrella; it might rain later.
rules.exampleIncorrect: Take an umbrella; it can rain later.

exercises.prompt: "Sarah just ran a 42km marathon. She ___ be exhausted!"
exercises.explanation: "Must" denotes high logical certainty based on strong evidence.

exercises.prompt: "Look at that old passport photo. That ___ be John; he looks completely different!"

title: Passive Voice Construction
description: Shift focus to the recipient or result of the action rather than the actor.
formula: Subject + [Be in right tense] + Past Participle (V3) + (by agent)

rules.title: When to Use Passive
rules.explanation: Use passive when the actor is unknown, obvious, or less important than the object affected.
rules.exampleCorrect: The Sydney Opera House was built in 1973.
rules.exampleIncorrect: Workers built the Sydney Opera House in 1973 (when focus is on the building).

rules.title: Tense Alignment
rules.explanation: The auxiliary verb 'be' carries the tense (is, was, has been, will be), followed by the V3 participle.
rules.exampleCorrect: The new bridge will be opened next Monday.
rules.exampleIncorrect: The new bridge will open by council next Monday.

exercises.prompt: "Millions of emails ___ around the world every single minute."
exercises.explanation: Present simple passive for habitual plural facts requires "are + sent".

title: Articles: A, An & The
description: Master specific vs. general noun determination in English speech.
formula: Indefinite (A/An) for non-specific, Definite (The) for specific or unique

rules.title: Sound, Not Letter
rules.explanation: Use 'an' before vowel sounds, not just vowel letters. E.g. 'an hour' (silent h), 'a university' (starts with /j/ consonant sound).
rules.exampleCorrect: It took an hour to finish the test.
rules.exampleIncorrect: It took a hour to finish the test.

rules.title: Unique Objects & Second Mentions
rules.explanation: Use 'the' for items that are unique (the sun, the internet) or have already been introduced previously in the discourse.
rules.exampleCorrect: I bought a coffee and a croissant. The coffee was delicious.
rules.exampleIncorrect: I bought a coffee. A coffee was delicious.

exercises.prompt: "He graduated with ___ degree in computer engineering."
exercises.explanation: "Degree" begins with a consonant sound, so "a degree" is correct.

exercises.prompt: "___ sun sets in the west every evening."
exercises.explanation: "The sun" is unique in our world, necessitating the definite article.
